references.text: The commandment to remember this day as a permanent statute, also mentioned in the Passover ordinance.
A night to be observed for the Lord, commemorating the exodus from Egypt.
God's strong hand that compelled Pharaoh to let the Israelites go.
The prohibition against eating leavened bread during the Feast of Unleavened Bread.
The Israelites baked unleavened bread because they were driven out of Egypt and had no time to let the dough rise.
A reminder that Israel was a slave in Egypt and that the Lord brought them out with a strong hand.
An exhortation to remember that they were slaves in Egypt and that the Lord brought them out with a strong hand.
The Lord brought Israel out of the house of slavery with a strong hand.
The commandment to eat unleavened bread for seven days to commemorate the exodus from Egypt.
God identifies Himself as the one who brought Israel out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
Paul quotes the institution of the Lord's Supper, where the unleavened bread takes on new meaning in Christ.
Both verses link the memory of the exodus from Egypt to bread and instructions for future generations.
Connects the prophecy about a hardened heart (4:21) with the completed exodus that is to be remembered (13:3).
The same law regarding unleavened bread and the remembrance of the exodus from Egypt given in two different contexts.
13:14 is the pedagogical implementation of the commandment to remember given in 13:3.
The manna in 16:6 serves as evidence of the same deliverance from Egypt mentioned in 13:3.
